item.title: England's university regulator calls for more assessment without AI and reopens the debate on how to verify authorship
item.description: The Office for Students recommends secure formats such as in-person or oral exams. In the group, members debated what can and cannot be detected.

media:content.media:description: A diagram in two halves: on the left, under the label “Secure formats”, three icons labelled “Oral” (a microphone), “Presentation” (a whiteboard) and “Practical” (a pencil); on the right, a magnifying glass crossed out in red with the label “Detector”.

item.title: Terminal or app: teachers compare ways of working with a coding agent
item.description: The group discussed whether the terminal offers more freedom than the graphical app, and concluded that it depends on the person and the task.

media:content.media:description: Three icons labelled “Web”, “App” and “Terminal” whose lines converge on a single box labelled “Result”.

item.title: An AI detector's percentage opens a conversation with the student, but does not prove they copied
item.description: A post on the blog “Familias con inteligencia” asks what to do when a detector flags the work of a student who says they wrote it themselves, and suggests backing the percentage up with evidence of the process.

media:content.media:description: A set of scales tipped to the right: on the lighter left pan, a card labelled “Detector 87%”; on the heavier right pan, another labelled “Drafts”, “Versions” and “Oral explanation”. Between the two pans, a magnifying glass and the label “A person decides”.

item.title: Teachers debate whether families’ authorisation is needed to use AI with students
item.description: One school has limited generative AI with its students because some families did not authorise it; other views hold that simply informing them is enough. The rules are clear: families must be informed, but between 14 and 18 their consent is not needed unless the tool requires it.

media:content.media:description: Infographic in two panels. On the left, “Under 14”, with a whiteboard and the label “In Catalonia, the teacher operates the AI”. On the right, “14 to 18”, with four rows: a megaphone, “Inform: always”; a pair of scales, “Consent: not needed”; a document with a tick, “Authorisation: advised in Catalonia”; and a document with a pencil, “Compulsory if the tool requires it”. Below, a band with a crossed-out person: “If a family objects, it only affects their child”.

item.title: Teachers debate Google’s announcement that switches off AI and search by default in school accounts
item.description: Google has announced that Gemini and Google Search will be switched off in primary and secondary school student accounts until administrators turn them on. In the groups, the news sparked a discussion about who decides how AI is used in a school.

media:content.media:description: On the left, an all-or-nothing master switch crossed out with a red X; on the right, four individual switches (Gemini, Notebook, Classroom and Search), two switched on in blue and two off.

item.title: Teachers as designers of learning are at the heart of the debate on AI in the classroom
item.description: After a conference on AI and education, members ask whether teachers stop being a source of information and how to prevent students from delegating their reasoning.

media:content.media:description: On the left, “Source”: a teacher transmits information with arrows towards three students; on the right, “Designer and guide”: another teacher with a question mark designs a route of stages leading to a flag labelled “Critical judgement”.

item.title: Publishing industry warns of a “witch hunt” over AI text detectors
item.description: A La Vanguardia report describes accusations of AI use based on detectors whose verdicts contradict themselves over time. The debate reaches education: how to check authorship without hunting for culprits.

media:content.media:description: Scales weighing, in one pan, “Detector”, an AI detector report marked with a question mark, and in the other, “Conversation and rules”, a conversation with the person and clear rules of use; below, a magnifying glass and the label “Indication, not proof”.

item.title: A publication offers guidance to families when AI does the homework
item.description: Chema Falcó proposes a simple test and a shared rule for telling apart using AI to learn from handing the learning over to it.

media:content.media:description: Three steps linked by arrows: “Think”, with a pencil; “Ask”, with a speech bubble; and “Check”, with a tick; below, a student explaining a homework sheet, “In your own words”.
